topics.title: The world ocean and the ocean floor

learn.hook: If you dropped Mount Everest into the deepest part of the ocean, its peak would still be under about 2 km of water!
points: About 71% of the Earth's surface is covered by water, and about 97% of all the Earth's water is in the salty oceans.
There are five oceans: Pacific (largest and deepest), Atlantic, Indian, Southern and Arctic (smallest). The Indian Ocean is the only ocean named after a country.
Continental shelf: the shallow, gently sloping edge of a continent under the sea. It is rich in fish and often in oil and gas, like Mumbai High off the coast of Maharashtra.
Continental slope: the steep drop from the shelf to the deep ocean. Deep-sea (abyssal) plains: huge, very flat areas covered with fine sediment.

Trenches are the deepest parts of the ocean; the Mariana Trench in the Pacific is about 11 km deep. Mid-ocean ridges are long underwater mountain chains, seamounts are underwater mountains that do not reach the surface, and atolls are ring-shaped coral islands around a lagoon, like many in Lakshadweep.

example.q: Think it through: Mount Everest is about 8,849 m high and the deepest point of the Mariana Trench is about 11,000 m deep. Would Everest stick out if placed in the trench?
steps: Compare the depth with the height: 11,000 m is more than 8,849 m.
Difference: 11,000 − 8,849 = 2,151 m, which is about 2 km.
So the top of Everest would still be about 2 km under water.
example.answer: No. Its peak would be about 2 km below the sea surface.

learn.reallife: Fishing boats from Kerala and Gujarat work mostly over the continental shelf, and the oil rigs of Mumbai High stand on it too.

games.title: Oceans by size
games.prompt: Arrange the oceans from largest to smallest

games.title: Ocean floor features
pairs: Shallow, gently sloping edge of a continent
Steep drop to the deep ocean
Deepest, narrow part of the ocean
Underwater mountain that does not reach the surface
Ring-shaped coral island around a lagoon

quiz.q: Which is the largest and deepest ocean?
quiz.explain: The Pacific Ocean is the largest ocean and also has the deepest point, in the Mariana Trench.
quiz.mistake: Picks the ocean nearest to India

quiz.q: About what percentage of the Earth's surface is covered by water?
quiz.explain: About 71% of the surface is water and about 29% is land. The figure 97% is the share of all water that is in the oceans.
quiz.mistake: Swaps the land and water shares, or mixes up 71% with the 97% of water held in oceans

quiz.q: The deepest known part of the ocean is in the:
quiz.explain: The Mariana Trench in the western Pacific is about 11 km deep, the deepest place known in the oceans.
quiz.mistake: Confuses a ridge, which is a raised feature, with a trench

quiz.q: Which part of the ocean floor is the shallowest and lies next to the land?
quiz.explain: The continental shelf is the submerged edge of the continent. The ocean gets deeper along the slope and is deepest in trenches.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the order of the ocean floor features

quiz.q: Mumbai High, an important source of oil and natural gas, lies on the:
options: continental shelf of the Arabian Sea
shore of the Bay of Bengal
quiz.explain: Mumbai High is an offshore oil field on the shallow continental shelf west of Mumbai, in the Arabian Sea.
quiz.mistake: Does not know that offshore oil is found mostly on continental shelves

quiz.q: What is an atoll?
options: A ring-shaped coral island or reef around a lagoon
A volcano that has stopped erupting
A long chain of underwater mountains
quiz.explain: Atolls are built by corals and form a ring around a shallow lagoon. Many of the Lakshadweep islands are coral atolls.
quiz.mistake: Confuses atolls with trenches or ridges

quiz.q: Which is the only ocean named after a country?
quiz.explain: The Indian Ocean is named after India, the only ocean named after a country.
quiz.mistake: Thinks other ocean names also come from countries

quiz.q: An underwater mountain that rises from the sea floor but does not reach the surface is a:
quiz.explain: A seamount is usually an old volcano under the sea. A flat-topped seamount is called a guyot.
quiz.mistake: Confuses underwater mountains with coastal features

teach.ask: Gappu looks at the sea from Marina Beach: "Is the ocean just a big, flat-bottomed bowl of water?"
teach.praise: Wow! Under the waves there are shelves, slopes, flat plains, deep trenches and underwater mountains. The ocean floor is as bumpy as the land!
teach.nudge: But is the ocean floor the same depth everywhere? What do we find near the coast and in the deepest parts?

learn.hook: The sea at Puri rises and falls like it is breathing, and its water tastes salty. What makes the ocean salty and restless?
points: Salinity is the amount of salt dissolved in sea water. The average salinity of the oceans is about 35 parts per thousand, that is about 35 g of salt in 1,000 g of sea water.

High evaporation raises salinity; fresh water from rivers, rain and melting ice lowers it. The Bay of Bengal is less salty than the Arabian Sea because big rivers like the Ganga and Brahmaputra pour fresh water into it.
Most waves are made by wind blowing over the water. A tsunami is a series of giant waves usually caused by an earthquake under the sea, like the one on 26 December 2004.

Tides are the regular rise and fall of sea level, caused mainly by the pull of the Moon's gravity, helped by the Sun. Most coasts get two high tides and two low tides a day. Spring tides (highest) come at full moon and new moon; neap tides (lowest range) come when the Moon is at its quarters.

Ocean currents are streams of water flowing in a fixed direction. Warm currents flow from near the equator towards the poles (Gulf Stream); cold currents flow from the poles towards the equator (Labrador Current). Where they meet, fog forms and fish are plentiful. Currents in the north Indian Ocean change direction with the monsoon.

example.q: Think it through: Why are the highest tides seen on full moon and new moon days?
steps: Tides are caused by the gravity of the Moon and the Sun pulling on the oceans.
On full moon and new moon days the Sun, the Moon and the Earth are in a straight line.
Their pulls add together, so high tides are higher and low tides are lower. These are spring tides.
example.answer: Because the Sun, Moon and Earth are in line, so their pulls combine to give spring tides.

learn.reallife: Fishers in Odisha and Gujarat plan trips by the tide table, salt pans need sunny weather for evaporation, and ships use tides to enter ports.

games.title: Sea secrets: true or false?
items: The average salinity of the oceans is about 35 parts per thousand.
That is about 35 g of salt in every 1,000 g of sea water.
Tides are caused mainly by the wind.
Tides are caused mainly by the Moon's gravity, helped by the Sun. Wind makes waves.
Spring tides happen only in the spring season.
Spring tides happen twice every month, at full moon and new moon. The name has nothing to do with the season.
The Gulf Stream is a warm ocean current.
It carries warm water from the Gulf of Mexico across the Atlantic.
Fresh water from rivers lowers the salinity of the sea.
River water adds water but little salt, so the sea water near river mouths is less salty.
The Arabian Sea is less salty than the Bay of Bengal.
It is the other way round: the Bay of Bengal gets far more river water, so it is less salty.

items.text: Tides are caused mainly by the pull of the ___.
A tsunami is usually caused by an ___ under the sea.
Cold currents flow from the poles towards the ___.
When the Moon is at its quarters we get ___ tides.
High ___ makes sea water more salty.

quiz.q: The average salinity of ocean water is about how many parts per thousand?
quiz.explain: On average, 1,000 g of sea water contains about 35 g of dissolved salts.
quiz.mistake: Gets the scale wrong by a factor of ten

quiz.q: What mainly causes tides?
options: The pull of the Moon's gravity on the oceans
The heat of the Sun evaporating water
quiz.explain: The Moon's gravity pulls the ocean water, helped by the Sun, creating the regular rise and fall of the tides.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the cause of tides with the cause of waves

quiz.q: Spring tides occur:
options: on full moon and new moon days
on the days when the Moon is at its quarters
quiz.explain: At full moon and new moon, the Sun, Moon and Earth are in a line and their pulls add up, giving the highest tides.
quiz.mistake: Takes the word 'spring' to mean the season

quiz.q: Most ordinary sea waves are produced by:
quiz.explain: Wind drags the surface water and builds up waves. Stronger winds make bigger waves.
quiz.mistake: Confuses waves with tides

quiz.q: A tsunami is usually caused by:
quiz.explain: A sudden movement of the sea floor during an undersea earthquake pushes up huge amounts of water and creates a tsunami.
quiz.mistake: Thinks tsunamis are just very big tides or storm waves

quiz.q: The Gulf Stream is an example of:
quiz.explain: The Gulf Stream carries warm water from near the equator across the Atlantic towards north-western Europe.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up warm and cold currents

quiz.q: Which of these increases the salinity of sea water?
options: High evaporation in hot, dry areas
quiz.explain: Evaporation removes water but leaves the salt behind, so the remaining water becomes saltier.
quiz.mistake: Thinks adding water makes the sea saltier

quiz.q: Why is the Bay of Bengal less salty than the Arabian Sea?
options: It is much deeper than the Arabian Sea
It is closer to the Arctic Ocean
Large rivers like the Ganga and Brahmaputra pour fresh water into it
quiz.explain: The Bay of Bengal receives huge amounts of river water, which dilutes the salt in it.
quiz.mistake: Does not link river water with lower salinity

teach.ask: Gappu dips his toe in the sea: "Why is it salty, and why does the water come up the beach and go back again?"
teach.praise: Tweet tweet! The sea is salty with about 35 parts per thousand, the Moon's gravity makes tides, wind makes waves and currents carry water across the oceans!
teach.nudge: Close! What pulls the water up and down the beach every day? Is it the wind or something in the sky?

learn.hook: Every year, lakhs of olive ridley turtles crawl onto the beaches of Odisha to lay their eggs. The ocean is full of such amazing life!
points: Marine life ranges from tiny plankton to the blue whale, the largest animal known. Phytoplankton make food using sunlight, produce a large share of the Earth's oxygen and form the base of ocean food chains.

Coral reefs are built over many years by tiny animals called coral polyps. In India they are found in the Gulf of Mannar, the Gulf of Kachchh, Lakshadweep and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands. Very warm water can make corals lose their colour (bleaching).

Mangroves are salt-tolerant trees of coastal swamps with special breathing roots. They protect coasts from storms and erosion and are nurseries for fish. The Sundarbans in the Ganga-Brahmaputra delta is the largest mangrove forest in the world and a home of the Royal Bengal tiger.

Ocean resources: fish and seafood, salt (Gujarat is India's largest producer), oil and natural gas (Mumbai High), manganese-rich nodules on the deep sea floor, tidal and wave energy, and sea routes for trade. India's Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ) stretches 200 nautical miles from its coast.
Threats include plastic waste, oil spills, overfishing and warming seas. Seasonal fishing bans in the breeding season, protected marine areas and beach clean-ups help.

example.q: Think it through: A cyclone hits two villages on the Odisha coast. One has a thick mangrove forest in front of it, the other does not. Which village is likely to suffer less, and why?
steps: Mangrove trees have dense roots and branches that slow down waves and storm surges.
Their roots hold the soil and reduce coastal erosion.
So the waves reaching the village behind the mangroves are weaker.
example.answer: The village protected by mangroves, because they slow waves and hold the coast together.

learn.reallife: The salt in your kitchen probably came from the salt pans of Gujarat, and the fish curry of Kerala or Bengal depends on healthy seas.

quiz.q: What forms the base of most ocean food chains?
quiz.explain: Phytoplankton are tiny plant-like organisms that make food using sunlight. Almost all other sea creatures depend on them directly or indirectly.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the biggest animals are at the base of the food chain

quiz.q: Which is the largest animal known to have lived on the Earth?
quiz.explain: The blue whale is larger than any dinosaur known. Surprisingly, it feeds on tiny shrimp-like krill.
quiz.mistake: Picks the largest fish or land animal instead

quiz.q: Coral reefs are built by:
options: tiny sea animals called coral polyps
quiz.explain: Coral polyps make hard skeletons of calcium carbonate. Over many years these build up into reefs.
quiz.mistake: Thinks corals are rocks or plants rather than animals

quiz.q: Which of these is a coral reef area of India?
quiz.explain: India's main coral reefs are in the Gulf of Mannar, the Gulf of Kachchh, Lakshadweep and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands. The others are lakes.
quiz.mistake: Assumes any famous water body has coral reefs

quiz.q: The Sundarbans are best known as:
options: the largest mangrove forest in the world, home of the Royal Bengal tiger
a coral reef in the Arabian Sea
quiz.explain: The Sundarbans lie in the Ganga-Brahmaputra delta, shared by India and Bangladesh.
quiz.mistake: Does not know the location and type of the Sundarbans

quiz.q: How do mangrove forests help coastal people?
options: They reduce damage from storm waves and slow down coastal erosion
They remove all fish from the sea
quiz.explain: Mangroves slow down waves and their roots hold the soil, protecting the coast. They are also breeding grounds for fish.
quiz.mistake: Does not see the protective role of mangroves

quiz.q: India's Exclusive Economic Zone extends up to how many nautical miles from the coast?
quiz.explain: In its EEZ, up to 200 nautical miles from the coast, India has rights over fish, oil, gas and minerals. 12 nautical miles is the limit of territorial waters.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the EEZ with territorial waters

quiz.q: Why is a fishing ban followed along India's coasts for some weeks every year?
options: Because sea water becomes too salty
Because the tides stop during those weeks
To allow ships to carry more oil
To let fish breed and keep fish stocks healthy
quiz.explain: The ban falls in the breeding season so that young fish can grow, which prevents overfishing.
quiz.mistake: Does not link the ban with the breeding season and overfishing

teach.ask: Gappu asks: "What lives in the sea, and what useful things does the ocean give us?"
teach.praise: Squawk! From plankton to blue whales, coral reefs to mangroves, and salt, fish and oil for us. I will never throw plastic on the beach!
teach.nudge: Good! But what do we get from the sea, and how can we keep it healthy?
